title: Processes, threads, and context switches
summary: Explain what the kernel saves and what threads share.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A process gives a program an address space and resource ownership. Threads in one process share that address space and file descriptors but have distinct stacks, registers, and scheduling state. Isolation and concurrency are separate properties.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: A context switch saves execution state and schedules another runnable task. Switching address spaces can also affect translation caches. A blocked I/O thread consumes no CPU while waiting, but a busy loop competes for CPU time.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For an ARM64 toolchain incident, separate a compiler process crash from a worker-thread race. First capture the signal, stack, inputs, and reproducibility; do not infer a scheduler bug from a timing-sensitive failure alone.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Suppose a service receives 100 independent requests, each spending 10 ms computing and 90 ms waiting for I/O. Sequential execution takes roughly 10 seconds. With enough outstanding requests, one CPU can overlap waiting and approach a compute ceiling of 100 requests per second, before other overheads. This does not require 100 CPU cores: concurrency hides waiting, while parallel execution handles simultaneous computation. Draw a timeline for two requests to show the difference. Then change each request to 90 ms of computation. The CPU becomes the bottleneck, and adding waiting threads cannot create processor capacity.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Threads share more than convenient data: an invalid pointer in one thread can corrupt another thread’s state. Separate processes improve fault isolation but introduce communication and serialization costs. Many blocked threads can consume substantial stack and bookkeeping space; an event loop reduces that cost but must not execute long blocking work on its shared thread. A thread count is therefore not a performance goal. Diagnose runnable versus blocked tasks and the serial portion of work before increasing the pool. Always include the downstream system’s capacity when choosing concurrency.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Your producer-consumer program should terminate cleanly, deliver every item once, and handle an empty queue without spinning. Use a fixed input size and report wall-clock duration, process CPU time, and worker count. Repeat enough runs to notice variance. Explain why low CPU time with high wall time suggests waiting, and why a highly utilized CPU does not prove useful work. Include a shutdown case where the consumer is asleep.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Runnable > Running > Blocked > Runnable

questions.q: Does adding threads always reduce latency?
questions.a: No. Synchronization, contention, scheduling, and serial work can outweigh parallel gains. Measure the critical path.

questions.q: What survives a thread switch?
questions.a: Shared process memory remains; each thread resumes its own stack and register context.

questions.q: How would you distinguish concurrency from parallelism in this service?
questions.a: Concurrency means multiple requests are in progress. Parallelism means their computations execute simultaneously. Overlapping an I/O wait with computation demonstrates concurrency on one core.

questions.q: Why might a larger thread pool slow the service?
questions.a: It can increase context switching, lock contention, cache disruption, and pressure on dependencies. Compare completed work and tail latency while varying the pool size.

lab: Write a producer and consumer. Measure wall time and CPU time with a busy wait and a condition variable. Explain the difference.

title: Scheduling and throughput
summary: Compare latency, fairness, and utilization.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: CPU scheduling chooses among runnable tasks. Round robin improves responsiveness through preemption; shortest-job approaches can reduce mean waiting time when job sizes are known. Real schedulers must also manage priorities and fairness.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: A long CPU task can delay interactive work if it runs without preemption. A very short quantum increases scheduling overhead. Compare average wait, tail latency, and throughput rather than optimizing only one number.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Apply Little’s law only to a stable system: average concurrency equals throughput multiplied by average time in system. An ever-growing queue violates the steady-state assumption.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Consider three CPU jobs arriving at time zero with durations 2, 4, and 20 ms. FIFO in that order completes them at 2, 6, and 26 ms; mean turnaround is 34/3, about 11.33 ms. Reversing the order gives completions 20, 24, and 26 ms, averaging 23.33 ms. Both schedules perform 26 ms of work. Round robin with a 2 ms quantum lets all three start within 4 ms, improving initial responsiveness even though context switches can add overhead. This example separates response time, completion time, and total work instead of treating them as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Shortest-job scheduling needs information that is rarely exact and can disadvantage long jobs when short work arrives continuously. Priority scheduling can invert expectations when a high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task. Priority inheritance addresses a specific inversion mechanism, not every scheduling problem. In a service, queueing can dominate execution as utilization approaches saturation. A benchmark at ten percent utilization can therefore conceal severe latency at production load. Include bursty arrivals and a long job among short ones when evaluating responsiveness.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Produce a table containing arrival, first-run, completion, response, and turnaround for every job. Show a time-axis schedule and account for all CPU work. Add a stated context-switch cost, rerun the calculation, and explain which metric changes. Your result should identify one workload where round robin helps and one where its overhead hurts. Little’s law calculations must use the same time units and a stable measurement interval.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Arrival > Run queue > CPU slice > Completion

questions.q: Why can throughput improve while latency worsens?
questions.a: Batching amortizes overhead but makes requests wait longer before service.

questions.q: What is starvation?
questions.a: A runnable task waits indefinitely because other tasks repeatedly receive service; aging or fair scheduling can mitigate it.

questions.q: What is the difference between response and turnaround time?
questions.a: Response time measures until the job first receives service; turnaround measures until it finishes. A time-sharing policy can improve one while delaying the other.

questions.q: What does a queue that grows throughout the experiment imply?
questions.a: Arrival rate exceeds sustainable service rate over that interval, so steady-state averages and Little’s law estimates need careful interpretation.

lab: Simulate FIFO and round robin for jobs of 2, 4, and 20 units arriving together. Calculate turnaround and response times.

title: Virtual memory, paging, and TLBs
summary: Trace a load from virtual address to physical memory.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Virtual memory separates program addresses from physical frames. A page table maps virtual pages to frames and permission bits. The TLB caches translations, so a TLB miss and a page fault are different events.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: A TLB miss may be satisfied by a page-table walk while the page remains in RAM. A fault can represent demand allocation, copy-on-write, a missing page, or a permission violation; it does not necessarily require disk access.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For memory regressions, inspect working-set size, access locality, page faults, and allocation behavior. Huge pages can reduce translation pressure but create allocation and fragmentation tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: With 4 KiB pages, a virtual address can be split into a page number and a 12-bit offset. Address 0x12345 therefore has page number 0x12 and offset 0x345. If its page maps to physical frame 0xABC, the physical address is 0xABC345. The offset stays unchanged. Now imagine scanning one byte from each of 4,096 pages. That accesses only 4 KiB of payload but spans 16 MiB of virtual memory, potentially stressing translation capacity. Contrast that with reading 4 KiB contiguously, where the same payload occupies approximately one page.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Do not diagnose every latency spike as swapping. Page-table walks, cache misses, minor faults, major faults, and allocation zeroing have different mechanisms. Copy-on-write initially shares pages but a write may require allocation and copying. Huge pages reduce the number of translations but can waste space or complicate allocation. A memory-mapped file can still generate faults on first access, and mapping a large file does not mean all its contents are resident. Measure page size, residency, access pattern, and cold versus warm behavior before choosing a remedy.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Explain the address arithmetic without confusing bytes and pages. Your benchmark should keep total reads comparable while varying locality, and should include a warm-up policy. Record the allocation size and whether the test exceeds likely cache capacity. State which observations are directly measured and which are hypotheses. Propose a follow-up measurement that would distinguish translation pressure from data-cache pressure rather than claiming elapsed time alone proves either.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Virtual address > TLB / page table > Physical frame > Cache / RAM

questions.q: Is virtual memory just swap?
questions.a: No. It provides address translation, protection, sharing, and demand allocation even without swap.

questions.q: Why does sequential traversal often beat random traversal?
questions.a: It exploits cache locality and prefetching, often reducing cache and translation misses.

questions.q: Why is the page offset unchanged by translation?
questions.a: Pages and frames have the same size and alignment, so translation selects a frame while preserving the byte’s position within it.

questions.q: Can two processes map the same physical page?
questions.a: Yes, for shared memory or shared read-only code, while maintaining separate virtual mappings and permissions.

lab: Allocate a large array and compare sequential with randomized reads. Record size and timing; explain which measurements would distinguish cache from TLB effects.

title: Locks, atomics, and memory ordering
summary: Separate atomicity, visibility, and ordering.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A mutex protects an invariant across multiple operations. An atomic variable prevents torn or conflicting accesses to that variable under the language memory model. Atomicity alone does not automatically publish surrounding non-atomic data.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: A producer can write a payload and then release-store a ready flag; an acquire-load observing that store allows the consumer to see preceding writes. Incorrect relaxed ordering can fail even if a test happens to pass on one architecture.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Your ARM64 experience is a useful entry to weak ordering. Discuss the C++ memory model first, then compiler transformations and hardware behavior. A data race on ordinary C++ objects is undefined behavior.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Model a one-shot publisher with ordinary payload data and an atomic ready flag. Producer: write payload = 42, then ready.store(true, release). Consumer: wait until ready.load(acquire) is true, then read payload. When that acquire observes the release, prior producer writes are ordered before the consumer’s later read. Replacing both operations with relaxed ordering preserves the flag’s atomicity but removes this publication relationship. If the producer modifies the payload again, the one-shot reasoning no longer suffices: you need a protocol protecting subsequent writes and reads too.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A correct atomic protocol can still suffer false sharing when independent frequently written variables occupy one cache line. Padding can help but increases memory use and should follow a profile. Busy waiting can be appropriate for very short waits but wastes CPU and can delay the thread that must make progress. Lock-free algorithms also face memory reclamation and ABA-style hazards; a pointer returning to the same value does not prove the referenced object has the same lifetime. Prefer a simple correct invariant before attempting a specialized optimization.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Document precisely which state is protected by each mutex or atomic operation. Test concurrent producers, consumers, shutdown, and full-capacity behavior. Explain why each condition-variable wait uses a predicate and why checking it in a loop is necessary. A passing stress test is supporting evidence, not a proof of race freedom. Include a small happens-before explanation and one intentionally incorrect version whose flaw you can describe without relying on it to fail every run.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Write payload > Release flag > Acquire flag > Read payload

questions.q: Is volatile a replacement for synchronization?
questions.a: No. C++ volatile does not provide inter-thread atomicity or a happens-before relationship.

questions.q: When is a lock better than lock-free code?
questions.a: When invariants span multiple objects or simplicity matters; lock-free progress does not guarantee lower latency or less contention.

questions.q: Why must a condition-variable wait recheck its predicate?
questions.a: Wakeups can be spurious, and another thread may change the condition before the awakened thread reacquires the lock.

questions.q: What does acquire-release not guarantee?
questions.a: It does not make an arbitrary multi-variable algorithm correct. The intended acquire must observe the relevant release, and other conflicting accesses still need synchronization.

lab: Build a bounded queue with a mutex and condition variables. Document the protected invariant and test shutdown while producers are blocked.

title: Deadlocks and concurrency debugging
summary: Turn a hang into a wait-for graph.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no forced preemption of held resources, and a circular wait. Preventing one condition can prevent a class of deadlocks. Livelock is active work without progress; starvation is persistent denial of service.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Two threads acquiring A then B and B then A can deadlock. A global lock order removes the cycle. Timeouts help detection or recovery but need a safe rollback strategy; retry loops may merely create livelock.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For a production hang, capture all thread stacks and lock ownership before restarting. Identify which resource each thread holds and awaits. Distinguish a lock cycle from slow I/O or an exhausted worker pool.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Suppose thread T1 holds a roster lock and waits for a driver lock, while T2 holds the driver lock and waits for the roster lock. The wait-for graph has T1 → T2 → T1, a cycle. Requiring every operation to acquire the roster lock before the driver lock prevents this particular cycle. Now consider a pool of four workers: all four submit child jobs to the same pool and synchronously wait. The child jobs remain queued forever because no worker is available. No conventional mutex cycle is required; the scarce resource is worker capacity.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A lock-order repair must cover every path, including error handling and callbacks. Calling arbitrary user code while holding a lock can introduce hidden dependencies. A timeout may break a wait but leaves recovery questions: which mutations already occurred, which resources remain held, and is retry safe? Repeatedly abandoning and reacquiring locks can create livelock. Capturing only one thread’s stack hides the dependency graph, so obtain a coherent view of all relevant threads and external waits. Avoid restarting before collecting evidence when it is operationally feasible.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Your report should name each held and awaited resource, identify the complete cycle, and show why the proposed ordering removes it. Capture a before-and-after trace or stack snapshot from your disposable example. Test an error path as well as the happy path. For the worker-pool example, propose an asynchronous continuation or separate execution strategy and explain why merely doubling the pool postpones rather than fundamentally removes the failure pattern.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Thread A holds L1 > Waits for L2 > Thread B holds L2 > Waits for L1

questions.q: Does a timeout prove deadlock?
questions.a: No. A slow operation can time out without a dependency cycle.

questions.q: How can a thread pool deadlock?
questions.a: All workers may block awaiting tasks queued to the same exhausted pool.

questions.q: Can a single-threaded event loop deadlock logically?
questions.a: Yes. It can wait for a result whose completion requires that same loop to process another event, even without multiple OS threads.

questions.q: Why is consistent ordering stronger than random backoff?
questions.a: Ordering structurally excludes circular acquisition. Random backoff may reduce collisions but does not prove the dependency cycle cannot recur.

lab: Construct a two-lock cycle in a disposable program, capture stacks, then repair it with a consistent lock order.

title: Filesystems, durability, and Linux debugging
summary: Distinguish a successful write from durable storage.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A file descriptor identifies an open file description; the path is a name used for lookup. Buffered writes can return before data reaches stable storage. Filesystem journaling and application durability guarantees solve related but different problems.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: An atomic rename can publish a new file version, but crash durability can also require syncing file data and the parent directory. A write-ahead log persists recovery information before applying updates to durable pages.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For toolchain failures, reduce the input, compare compiler flags, inspect symbols and relocations, and preserve the failing binary. Correlate system calls, resource limits, and signal information instead of assuming every crash is a compiler defect.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: To replace a configuration file, create a temporary file in the same directory, write the complete new contents, synchronize the file, rename it over the destination, then synchronize the directory where supported and appropriate. A crash before publication should leave the old name; a crash afterward should expose the new complete version under the filesystem’s guarantees. Atomic visibility and crash durability are distinct. This sequence also needs permissions, error checks, and cleanup of abandoned temporary files. It is a reasoning model, not a universal promise for every filesystem, mount option, and storage device.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A short write requires writing the remaining bytes; assuming one call transfers the full buffer can silently truncate output. Interrupted operations and full disks need explicit handling. Memory mapping does not eliminate durability concerns, and storage devices may have caches with their own guarantees. For compiler debugging, stale build artifacts or mismatched libraries can imitate source defects. Record exact commands and versions, rebuild a minimal case, and compare one variable at a time. A workaround that disables optimization might mask undefined behavior rather than establish a compiler bug.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create a failure table for interruption before writing, during writing, after synchronization, after rename, and after directory synchronization. For each point, state which file version is allowed to appear and what assumption supports that statement. Your debugging record should include the smallest source input, complete compile command, observed failure, and expected result. A successful rerun alone is insufficient: explain the regression check that would catch recurrence.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: User buffer > Kernel page cache > Filesystem > Storage

questions.q: Does write returning imply power-loss durability?
questions.a: No. Data may still be buffered; explicit synchronization and storage guarantees matter.

questions.q: Why preserve a minimal reproducer?
questions.a: It separates environmental noise from the defect and makes regression testing and upstream reporting practical.

questions.q: Why synchronize a directory after rename?
questions.a: The directory contains the name-to-file mapping; persisting file contents alone does not necessarily persist the updated directory entry across a crash.

questions.q: What does a disappearing crash under optimization changes establish?
questions.a: Only that behavior is sensitive to the change. It may implicate undefined behavior, layout, timing, or compiler transformation and needs further isolation.

lab: Explain a crash-safe configuration-file update and list the failure points before and after rename.

title: Layers and the journey of a request
summary: Connect application behavior to network boundaries.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: An application sends bytes through transport, IP routing, and link-layer delivery. Each layer adds its own addressing and control information. TCP ports identify endpoints within a host; IP addresses support delivery across networks.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Opening a site can involve DNS, connection setup, TLS negotiation, request transmission, and response processing. Cached DNS or an existing connection can skip parts of this path, so a single latency figure hides several causes.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: When diagnosing a slow API, separate name resolution, connection establishment, time to first byte, and body download. A database bottleneck often appears as server waiting time rather than a slow packet transfer.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Assume DNS takes 20 ms, a new TCP handshake takes 40 ms, TLS setup adds 40 ms, server processing takes 80 ms, and transfer takes 10 ms. A simplified sequential budget totals 190 ms. Reusing a connection can remove much of the setup cost, while overlapping steps and protocol choices can change the real timeline. If a trace shows 85 ms until the server starts responding but only 5 ms transferring data, buying bandwidth is unlikely to fix the main delay. Break the measurement into phases before proposing an architectural change.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Layer diagrams are models, not proof that every request takes the same route. Proxies, VPNs, connection pools, and cached results alter the path. Application retries can create several network attempts for one user action. A successful TCP connection does not prove a service can process requests, and packet loss is not the only cause of slow responses. When comparing endpoints, control connection reuse, payload size, geography, and load. Otherwise a cold connection to one service and a warm connection to another produce a misleading comparison.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Your diagram must identify each component’s address or identity boundary and distinguish client-side from server-side waiting. Give every network hop a timeout owner. Include one scenario where DNS fails, one where the connection fails, and one where the application is slow despite a healthy connection. Explain which observation would distinguish these cases and show how a trace identifier follows the request into the service and its database call.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: DNS > Transport > TLS > HTTP > Service

questions.q: Is a port an application identity?
questions.a: It is a transport endpoint number; processes can bind or share endpoints under operating-system rules.

questions.q: Why can ping succeed while HTTPS fails?
questions.a: They exercise different protocols, ports, policies, and application paths.

questions.q: Why should end-to-end latency be measured as well as server latency?
questions.a: Users also experience DNS, connection setup, network transfer, queues, and client processing that a server-only measurement omits.

questions.q: Can a slower first request be normal?
questions.a: Yes. Cold DNS, connection setup, TLS, cache population, and runtime initialization can add work absent from subsequent requests.

lab: Draw a browser-to-FastAPI request, including DNS, load balancer, service, and database. Mark each timeout boundary.

title: TCP reliability and congestion control
summary: Explain sequencing without promising message boundaries.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission and flow control. Sequence numbers identify byte positions. Applications must frame messages themselves because one send call need not correspond to one receive call.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Flow control protects the receiver using its advertised window. Congestion control responds to network conditions using a congestion window. Throughput can be constrained by either window and the round-trip time.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: A timeout does not reveal whether the server committed an operation. Retrying a payment therefore requires an application-level idempotency key even though the transport is reliable.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A sender with 64 KiB of usable in-flight data and a 100 ms round-trip time has an approximate window-limited ceiling of 655,360 bytes per second, about 0.625 MiB/s, before overhead and losses. A faster link alone cannot remove that limit. Separately, suppose send writes HELLO followed by WORLD. The receiver may observe HE, LLOWOR, and LD, or the entire ten bytes at once. Prefixing each message with its length lets the receiver accumulate bytes until a complete application message exists. Reliability does not preserve the sender’s write boundaries.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A connection reset leaves the application uncertain about which operations the peer processed. A reliable transport cannot resolve whether a payment committed just before the response was lost. Application deadlines may expire while packets are still being retransmitted. Flow control and congestion control should not be confused: a small receiver window reflects receiver capacity, while congestion control addresses the network path. Very large buffers can increase queueing delay. Tune based on throughput and latency together, and avoid treating retransmission counts as a complete diagnosis without the surrounding traffic pattern.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Your framing implementation must parse a split header, a split payload, two concatenated messages, and an invalid length. Set a maximum accepted message size so a corrupt header cannot request unbounded allocation. Demonstrate that incomplete data waits rather than being mistaken for a complete message. For the throughput calculation, state byte units and RTT explicitly, then explain one reason observed performance could fall below the window-based estimate.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Bytes > Segments > Acknowledgments > Retransmission

questions.q: Does TCP guarantee a business action happens once?
questions.a: No. It transports bytes; application retries and crash recovery determine business semantics.

questions.q: Why does high RTT limit throughput?
questions.a: The sender can have only a bounded amount of unacknowledged data in flight; small windows relative to bandwidth-delay product underutilize the link.

questions.q: Why is application framing necessary on TCP?
questions.a: TCP delivers an ordered stream of bytes, so the receiver needs an independent rule for identifying complete application messages.

questions.q: Can an HTTP timeout prove a write was not applied?
questions.a: No. The server may commit before the response arrives; use an idempotency key or a status lookup to resolve ambiguity.

lab: Implement newline-delimited messages and test a message split across multiple reads and multiple messages in one read.

title: DNS, caching, and load balancing
summary: Understand why an address change is not instant.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: DNS resolves names through a hierarchy and caches responses. A TTL bounds a cache entry’s intended lifetime; recursive resolvers and client caches introduce different places where old answers may persist.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Layer-4 balancing routes connections using transport information. Layer-7 balancing can inspect application requests and route by path or headers. Health checks must reflect useful service capacity rather than merely an open port.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: During an outage, compare DNS answers, resolver choice, TTLs, backend health, and connection reuse. A healthy load balancer cannot compensate for all backends failing the same database dependency.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Imagine a DNS record cached at 12:00 with a 300-second TTL. Changing the authoritative answer at 12:01 does not necessarily change that resolver’s answer immediately; its existing entry may remain usable until approximately 12:05. Meanwhile a client using an established connection may not resolve again at all. For a load-balanced service with three backends, route one request to each and compare readiness checks with real work. If all report healthy while their database pool is exhausted, a simple process-alive endpoint has failed to represent serving capacity.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Aggressively short TTLs increase lookup traffic and do not guarantee instantaneous traffic migration. Sticky sessions simplify affinity but can create imbalance and complicate failover. Removing a backend from rotation does not necessarily terminate in-flight work; draining policy matters. Health checks that depend on every optional downstream service can remove otherwise useful capacity, while checks that ignore critical dependencies can send traffic to unusable nodes. Define what the service can still do under partial failure, and make readiness reflect that product behavior rather than an arbitrary all-or-nothing dependency list.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: List the authoritative record, recursive cache, client cache, and live connection separately in your incident timeline. Show the old and new address with the intended TTL. Define a readiness endpoint for retrieval traffic and explain its behavior when embeddings are unavailable but cached answers exist. The rubric should distinguish genuinely degraded service from a dead process and include a draining sequence that lets an in-flight request complete.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Client cache > Recursive resolver > Authoritative DNS > Load balancer

questions.q: Does DNS balancing move an established connection?
questions.a: No. Existing connections generally continue using their selected endpoint.

questions.q: What is a misleading health check?
questions.a: A check that reports healthy while critical dependencies or worker capacity prevent real requests from succeeding.

questions.q: Why can two users see different backends after a DNS change?
questions.a: They may use different caches with different remaining lifetimes, or reuse connections created before the change.

questions.q: What is the tradeoff in dependency-aware readiness?
questions.a: It avoids routing to unusable instances but can remove all capacity during a shared dependency failure unless useful degraded behavior is considered.

lab: Design health checks for a RAG API: separate process liveness from readiness to serve retrieval traffic.

title: HTTP, caching, and API semantics
summary: Use methods and cache rules intentionally.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: HTTP method semantics distinguish safe operations and idempotent effects. Idempotence means repeating a request has the same intended effect, not that each response is identical. POST needs application design when retry safety matters.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Conditional requests can use entity tags to avoid transferring unchanged representations. Cache keys must account for relevant request variants and authorization. Accidentally caching a private response for another user is a correctness failure.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For a study-progress API, a version or entity tag can detect concurrent updates from two devices. Decide whether conflicts merge individual problem states or reject stale whole-document writes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A learner reads progress version 7 with ETag "v7". Two devices edit that snapshot. Device A sends PUT with If-Match: "v7" and succeeds, creating version 8. Device B sends the same precondition and receives a precondition-failed response instead of overwriting A’s update. B can fetch version 8 and merge independent problem states. If both changed the same note, the product needs a conflict policy. This is optimistic concurrency: it allows normal independent work while detecting a stale write at the actual update boundary.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Cache correctness depends on representation identity. A response varying by language or authorization cannot safely share a key that ignores those dimensions. Returning the same status code for all errors also makes retry policy difficult: invalid input, conflict, and temporary unavailability need different responses. Idempotence is about intended effect, so charging twice with the same arbitrary POST body is not automatically safe. Design explicit keys and retention rules when retries must deduplicate. Avoid logging full request bodies containing private code or notes merely to debug a cache issue.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Provide concrete example requests and responses for reading, updating, and rejecting a stale progress version. Specify whether a missing precondition is accepted. Test two simulated clients and show that one update is not silently lost. For caching, list the exact key fields and freshness rule for a public lesson. Explain why private progress uses a different policy, and identify a test that would detect one learner receiving another learner’s data.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Request > Cache validation > Origin > Representation

questions.q: Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?
questions.a: It can be: the intended final state remains absence even when status codes differ.

questions.q: Why use optimistic concurrency?
questions.a: It detects lost updates without holding a long-lived lock across user interactions.

questions.q: Why can a conflict need product-level resolution?
questions.a: The server can detect concurrent edits but may not know which of two competing note changes the user intends to keep.

questions.q: How does conditional GET differ from conditional PUT?
questions.a: A conditional GET can avoid retransferring an unchanged representation; a conditional PUT can prevent updating a representation that changed since it was read.

lab: Specify GET and PUT for study progress, including version checks, status codes, and a conflict example.

title: TLS, authentication, and trust
summary: Separate encryption from application authorization.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: TLS protects a connection’s confidentiality and integrity and authenticates peers according to its configuration. A certificate binds an identity to a public key through a trust system; encryption alone does not establish that an endpoint is the intended one.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Authentication answers who is calling. Authorization decides which resources and actions that identity can access. A valid signed token does not eliminate the need to check tenant, scope, expiry, and resource ownership.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Keep service credentials on a trusted backend, restrict their permissions, and rotate them. A browser bundle is public to its users, so embedding an API secret there does not keep it secret.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Suppose user A requests GET /notes/42 with a valid token. The server verifies the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry, then loads note 42 and checks its owner or shared-access policy. If note 42 belongs only to B, the request must fail even though A is authenticated. TLS protects the connection carrying the token but does not supply this ownership check. In a service-to-service call, also separate the calling service’s identity from the end user’s authority; possession of a backend credential must not automatically grant access to every tenant’s records.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Token storage, replay, revocation, and logging each create separate risks. A long-lived token remains useful to anyone who obtains it until it expires or is invalidated under the system’s design. A certificate error should not be bypassed merely to make a request succeed. Conversely, encrypting internal traffic does not fix excessive database privileges. Start from the required action and grant the minimum resources needed. Test denied requests as carefully as allowed ones, because a system that always permits access can appear perfectly functional in happy-path testing.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create an authorization matrix with owner, shared reader, unrelated user, and unauthenticated caller. For each, specify read and write outcomes. Add tests for an expired token and an otherwise valid token with the wrong audience. Draw where the browser can see data and where the server keeps secrets. Your explanation should identify what TLS guarantees and what remains an application responsibility without treating encryption as a universal security solution.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Handshake > Identity validation > Encrypted channel > Authorization

questions.q: Does HTTPS prevent insecure direct object references?
questions.a: No. The application must verify that the caller may access the requested object.

questions.q: Why is a valid JWT insufficient by itself?
questions.a: The server must also verify issuer, audience, expiry, signature policy, and authorization for the operation.

questions.q: Why should authorization be checked for every object?
questions.a: A caller can change an identifier independently of the UI; object ownership and sharing rules must be enforced at the data-access boundary.

questions.q: Why should a backend credential have narrow privileges?
questions.a: If it leaks or a component misuses it, least privilege limits which resources and actions are exposed.

lab: Threat-model a shared preparation app: identify which data is local, which crosses the network, and which operations need authorization.

title: Relational modeling and normalization
summary: Design constraints before optimizing queries.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A relation describes records with attributes; keys identify rows and foreign keys constrain relationships. Normalization reduces update anomalies by separating facts with different dependencies. It is a design tool, not a rule to split every table.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: For a bus roster, store driver identity separately from assignments. A unique constraint can prohibit duplicate assignments for the same slot, while temporal overlap rules may need richer constraints or transactional validation.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Denormalization can make reads cheaper but creates duplicated facts and repair work. State the workload and consistency requirement before adding cached counts or repeated descriptive fields.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Use Driver(driver_id, name), Bus(bus_id, capacity), Shift(shift_id, start_at, end_at), and Assignment(driver_id, shift_id, bus_id). Storing the driver’s name in every assignment duplicates a fact that depends on driver_id, creating inconsistency when a name changes. A unique key on (driver_id, shift_id) prevents duplicate assignments to exactly the same shift identifier. It does not prevent overlapping shifts with different identifiers. Write the actual business invariant in time terms before deciding whether a unique constraint is sufficient; naming a row uniquely and ruling out overlapping intervals are different requirements.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Over-normalization can make common reads expensive and produce complicated joins, but denormalization should have a maintenance strategy. A cached bus capacity copied into an assignment might intentionally represent capacity at booking time rather than the bus’s current capacity; semantics determine whether duplication is wrong. NULL values also need explicit meaning: unknown, not applicable, and absent are not always interchangeable. Schema changes must consider historical records and migration behavior. Before adding a field, state whether it is a current fact, a historical snapshot, or a derived value.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Write a compact schema with keys and foreign-key directions, then insert examples that should be accepted and rejected. Include two overlapping shifts with different identifiers to demonstrate the limits of simple uniqueness. Show how a driver name change affects the normalized design. For any deliberately duplicated field, name the source of truth and update rule. Your answer should explain one justified denormalization instead of claiming that every duplicated value is automatically an error.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Facts > Dependencies > Tables > Constraints

questions.q: What is an update anomaly?
questions.a: Duplicated facts can diverge when one copy changes and another does not.

questions.q: Can application checks replace constraints?
questions.a: They can race under concurrency; database constraints provide a final enforcement boundary.

questions.q: Can duplicated data ever be intentional?
questions.a: Yes. A historical snapshot or a maintained read model may deliberately duplicate a value, provided its semantics and update policy are clear.

questions.q: Why does UNIQUE(driver_id, shift_id) not prevent all scheduling conflicts?
questions.a: Two distinct shift IDs can cover overlapping time intervals, so the uniqueness key does not express the temporal invariant.

lab: Model drivers, shifts, buses, and assignments. Identify primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness, and the overlap invariant.

title: Indexes and query plans
summary: Explain both the benefit and the write cost.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A B-tree index supports ordered lookup and range access. A composite index is ordered by its key sequence, which affects how predicates and sorting can use it. Indexes consume space and add work to inserts and updates.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: For WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, an index beginning with user_id followed by created_at can reduce scanning. A low-selectivity predicate may still be cheaper as a sequential scan.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Read estimated versus actual row counts in an execution plan. Large differences can indicate stale statistics or correlated predicates. Distinguish time spent scanning, sorting, joining, and waiting.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: For attempts(user_id, created_at, status, code), consider SELECT created_at, status FROM attempts WHERE user_id = 17 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. A B-tree on (user_id, created_at DESC) groups that user’s entries in useful order, allowing an early stop after enough rows. An index only on status may examine many rows because most attempts share a few statuses. If the query selects a large code column, heap access and transferred bytes may dominate even after filtering improves. Compare row estimates, actual rows, and buffers to understand where the index helps.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: An index’s usefulness depends on selectivity, ordering, table size, and the requested columns. A planner can reasonably choose a sequential scan for a small table or a broad predicate. Repeatedly benchmarking the same query warms caches, so an apparent improvement may reflect memory residency. Functions or casts applied to indexed columns can change whether an index is usable. Every extra index also increases write maintenance. Avoid forcing plans before investigating stale statistics, skew, or correlated filters; a forced plan that helps one parameter value can harm another.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create a baseline plan and an indexed plan using the same data and query semantics. Include at least one highly active learner and one with very few attempts to expose skew. Report actual rows, sort behavior, and buffer activity where available. Demonstrate a query the index does not help and explain why. Your conclusion must account for insertion overhead and storage cost, not merely announce that the faster read means the index is universally better.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Query > Planner > Index / scan > Rows

questions.q: Why not index every column?
questions.a: Storage, cache pressure, and maintenance costs can outweigh read benefits.

questions.q: Does a sequential scan always mean a bad plan?
questions.a: No. Reading a large share of a table can make sequential access efficient.

questions.q: Why does column order matter in a composite B-tree?
questions.a: The entries are ordered lexicographically, so the leading key strongly influences which ranges can be located and scanned efficiently.

questions.q: What does a large estimated-versus-actual row mismatch suggest?
questions.a: The planner’s selectivity model may be inaccurate due to statistics, skew, or correlations, potentially leading to a poor join or access strategy.

lab: Create a progress table with 100,000 rows and compare plans before and after a composite index. Explain rows examined, not only elapsed time.

title: Transactions, isolation, and MVCC
summary: Reason about anomalies with concrete interleavings.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Atomicity groups changes, consistency preserves declared invariants, isolation controls concurrent effects, and durability concerns committed state surviving failures. These properties do not make every business invariant automatic.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: MVCC lets readers view versions rather than always blocking writers. Snapshot-style isolation can still permit write skew when transactions update different rows based on a shared predicate. Serializable execution or explicit coordination may be needed.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For two on-call drivers, both transactions might observe another available driver and independently mark themselves unavailable. The invariant spans rows, so locking only each modified row is insufficient.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Use doctors(id, on_call) with two rows initially true. In PostgreSQL, session A runs BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call; and sees 2. Session B does the same and also sees 2. A executes UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE id = 1; B updates id = 2; both can commit, leaving zero on call. Under SERIALIZABLE, one transaction can be aborted to prevent the unsafe history. The application must retry the entire transaction, including the count, rather than blindly replay only its final update.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Locking only the row being changed does not protect a predicate spanning other rows. One alternative is a shared coordination row that every relevant transaction locks before checking coverage; this can serialize work but may become a hotspot. Serializable isolation is powerful but requires retry handling and performance evaluation. External effects such as sending an email should not be performed irreversibly inside a transaction that might retry. Use an outbox or another explicit mechanism so a database abort does not leave a successful external side effect disconnected from committed state.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Write the two-session timeline with every read, update, and commit. Reproduce the anomaly in an isolated database, then apply either serializable isolation or a consistent locking strategy. Verify the invariant after both sessions finish and explain the retry path. Include a test where one session aborts. Your success criterion is preservation of at least one on-call row, not merely the absence of database errors or the completion of both original requests.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Read snapshot > Validate invariant > Write > Commit / retry

questions.q: What is write skew?
questions.a: Concurrent transactions read a shared condition and update different records, jointly violating an invariant.

questions.q: Why retry serialization failures?
questions.a: The database rejected an unsafe interleaving; restarting the complete transaction can produce a valid serial outcome.

questions.q: Why must a serialization retry include the reads?
questions.a: Those reads established the decision using an obsolete concurrent view. Repeating only the write can preserve the same invalid decision.

questions.q: Why are external side effects difficult inside retrying transactions?
questions.a: They may succeed even when the database transaction aborts, and a retry can repeat them. Coordinate their publication with committed state.

lab: Write an interleaving for two drivers going off duty. Show why row-level updates can violate coverage and propose a repair.

title: SQL joins, windows, and analytical thinking
summary: Choose operations by row semantics.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: An inner join returns matching combinations; a left join preserves unmatched left rows. Duplicate join keys multiply rows, so an unexpected count often reflects cardinality rather than a database error.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. Window functions retain rows while calculating over partitions. Ranking functions differ on ties: row_number assigns unique positions, rank leaves gaps, and dense_rank does not.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For daily study streaks, define timezone and whether multiple attempts count once per day. A correct query begins with a clear event definition; otherwise a sophisticated window expression answers the wrong question.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Latest attempt per learner can be expressed as SELECT * FROM (SELECT user_id, problem_id, submitted_at, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY submitted_at DESC, attempt_id DESC) AS rn FROM attempts) t WHERE rn = 1. The attempt_id tie-breaker makes selection deterministic when timestamps match. For top scores with ties, use DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY score DESC) and filter rank <= 3 if three distinct score levels are intended. That may return more than three rows. State whether the requirement concerns rows, ranks, or distinct score levels.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Joining attempts to a table with multiple tags per problem multiplies each attempt, potentially inflating counts. Aggregate at the intended grain or use EXISTS when you only need membership. In a left join, WHERE attempts.status = 'passed' discards learners with no attempt; placing that filter in ON preserves them. COUNT(*) counts the preserved row, while COUNT(attempts.attempt_id) ignores its NULL right side. Timezone conversion must occur before grouping into user-local calendar days if that is the product’s definition of a study day.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Build a tiny dataset containing a learner with no attempts, equal timestamps, tied scores, and a problem with two tags. Show expected rows before running the query. Explain why your latest-attempt ordering is deterministic and why your ranking query can return more than three rows. Verify the empty-learner case with COUNT of a nullable joined key. A successful query must match the specified row grain, not just produce syntactically valid SQL.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Filter > Join > Group / window > Order

questions.q: Why can a WHERE clause undo a left join?
questions.a: Filtering a nullable right-side field can discard unmatched rows; place the intended condition in the join or handle NULL explicitly.

questions.q: When use a window instead of GROUP BY?
questions.a: When each original row must remain visible beside a partition-level calculation.

questions.q: Why include attempt_id in the latest-row ordering?
questions.a: Equal timestamps otherwise leave the chosen row unspecified; a stable unique tie-breaker makes results reproducible.

questions.q: Why can COUNT(*) return one for a learner with no attempts after a left join?
questions.a: The left join preserves one row with NULL right-side fields. COUNT(*) counts that row, whereas COUNT of the right-side key does not.

lab: Write queries for each learner’s latest attempt, top three scores with ties, and days with no attempts. Explain duplicate handling.

title: Row stores, column stores, and ClickHouse
summary: Defend a migration using workload evidence.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Row-oriented storage places fields of a record together and suits many point updates and transactional access patterns. Column-oriented storage enables scanning selected columns and compression over similar values, which suits analytical aggregation.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: ClickHouse uses sparse primary indexes over sorted data rather than assuming one index entry per row. Choosing an ordering key affects how much data can be skipped for frequent filters. It should follow measured access patterns.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For your migration story, report query shapes, volume, ingestion cadence, p95 latency, correctness checks, and rollback design. A speedup is only meaningful with comparable hardware, data, cache state, and query semantics.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Suppose a telemetry table has 100 million rows and 20 equally sized fields, but a report needs only route_id and duration. Ignoring compression and metadata, reading two columns can reduce the scanned field volume to one tenth of a full-row scan. If data is sorted by (route_id, event_time), a query for one route and a time range may skip irrelevant blocks. A query filtering only an unrelated driver field may benefit much less. The example motivates column pruning and sort-key choice; it is not a promise of a tenfold end-to-end speedup.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Analytical speed can come with different update, constraint, and transaction behavior from an OLTP database. Frequent tiny changes, late-arriving events, and deduplication need an explicit model. A sparse index identifies candidate ranges, so some rows within those ranges still require inspection. Benchmarking only one popular query can overfit the physical design. Include ingestion cost, storage compression, concurrency, and recovery alongside read latency. A migration that returns faster but different totals has failed; reconcile semantics such as timezones, NULL treatment, duplicates, and numeric precision.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create a benchmark matrix with at least three query shapes: route/time filtering, broad aggregation, and a less favorable filter. Document data size, hardware, concurrency, warm-up, and cache policy. Compare exact counts and totals on the same event set before comparing latency. Include duplicate and late events, then demonstrate how the new pipeline handles them. Finish with a rollback trigger that names a correctness or performance threshold rather than a vague impression.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Events > Column blocks > Data skipping > Aggregation

questions.q: Is an analytical store a drop-in OLTP replacement?
questions.a: Usually not; update patterns, constraints, transactions, and latency goals must be evaluated.

questions.q: What migration evidence is persuasive?
questions.a: Reproducible before-and-after measurements plus reconciliation, failure handling, and a rollback path.

questions.q: Why might the same sort key help one query and hurt another?
questions.a: It clusters data along chosen dimensions, improving pruning for aligned predicates while leaving unrelated predicates with larger scans.

questions.q: Why distinguish scanned bytes from end-to-end latency?
questions.a: Network transfer, aggregation, decompression, queueing, and result rendering can dominate even when fewer bytes are read.

lab: Design a benchmark for roster analytics with cold and warm runs. Include counts, sums, late events, and duplicate ingestion checks.

title: Replication, sharding, and recovery
summary: State what happens when a node fails.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Replication keeps multiple copies; sharding partitions ownership. Replicas can serve reads or improve availability, while shards distribute storage and write load. Neither automatically solves skew or guarantees fresh reads.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Asynchronous replication can expose stale data and lose recent acknowledged writes if the primary fails before replication. Synchronous acknowledgment changes the latency and availability tradeoff; the exact guarantee depends on which replicas acknowledge.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: A backup is useful only if restore is tested. Define recovery point objective for acceptable data loss and recovery time objective for acceptable outage duration. Replicas also replicate accidental deletions.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A primary acknowledges writes W1, W2, and W3, but its asynchronous replica has applied only W1 when the primary fails. Promoting that replica can lose W2 and W3 unless another recovery source retains them. If the business permits at most one minute of loss, replication lag must be interpreted against that recovery-point goal, not merely displayed as a graph. For recovery time, add detection, failover decision, promotion, client reconnection, and validation. A five-second database promotion does not imply the entire application recovers in five seconds.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Synchronous replication can reduce acknowledged-write loss under its stated failure model but may block writes when required replicas are unavailable. Read replicas introduce freshness concerns, and sharding creates cross-shard operations and skew. Choosing a shard key with a few dominant customers can overload one shard despite ample aggregate capacity. Backups need independent retention and restore testing because accidental deletion, corruption, or malicious changes can propagate through replicas. Recovery procedures should include credentials, schema versions, and application compatibility rather than only copying database files.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Define RPO and RTO in concrete units and distinguish a target from a demonstrated result. Your drill should record a known write sequence, simulate loss of the primary, restore or promote, and compare surviving records. Measure the time until useful application requests succeed. Include a logical-deletion scenario to show why a replica is insufficient. Describe how clients avoid continuing to write to an old primary after a failover decision.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Primary > Replication log > Replica > Restore checkpoint

questions.q: Why might read-after-write fail?
questions.a: A subsequent read may reach a replica that has not applied the write.

questions.q: Why is replication not a backup?
questions.a: Corruption or deletion can propagate to replicas; independent historical recovery is still needed.

questions.q: What is replication lag actually measuring?
questions.a: It may mean time, log position, or unapplied work depending on the metric. Interpret the specific metric before translating it into possible data loss.

questions.q: Why is a shard key hard to change later?
questions.a: It determines data placement and routing, so changing it can require large data movement, dual routing, and consistency management during migration.

lab: Design a recovery drill for payment records and document which acknowledged operations could be missing after failover.

title: Requirements and capacity estimates
summary: Turn an open question into explicit constraints.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Begin with users, actions, scale, correctness, and latency. Separate functional behavior from availability and operational goals. A design for a two-person local study app differs radically from a public coding judge.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Estimate peak requests, payload sizes, storage growth, and concurrency using visible assumptions. Convert units carefully: daily traffic is not peak traffic, and compressed storage differs from raw event size.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Draw the simplest design meeting the constraints, then identify the first bottleneck. An interviewer should see why each queue, cache, or shard exists rather than a list of fashionable components.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: One million learners making ten attempts daily create ten million attempts per day, averaging about 116 attempts per second. If peak traffic is eight times average, plan initially for roughly 930 attempts per second. At 2 KiB per stored attempt, raw daily growth is about 19 GiB before indexes, replication, and backups. Retaining code snapshots at 20 KiB increases the estimate by tenfold. These are assumptions to validate. Separate read traffic, execution jobs, and saved attempts because one page view may cause several requests while one coding attempt may consume seconds of CPU.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Averages hide bursts and skew. Some learners submit large code files, and a small number of popular problems can dominate reads. Executing untrusted code changes the problem: process isolation, resource limits, and abuse prevention become core requirements rather than optional polish. A two-person local app can use a simple local architecture, while a public judge needs a separate execution boundary. Avoid carrying every large-scale component into a small system. State which trigger would justify introducing a queue, replica, cache, or shard.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Provide an assumptions table with users, actions per day, peak factor, payload size, and retention. Show unit conversions and a low/high estimate for uncertain inputs. Draw a baseline architecture and label where CPU-heavy execution differs from ordinary content delivery. Identify the first likely bottleneck and propose a measurement to validate it. Your design should also explain how a single-user local version remains useful without operating the full large-scale architecture.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Requirements > Estimates > Baseline > Bottleneck > Tradeoff

questions.q: Why estimate before choosing a database?
questions.a: Workload shape and scale determine which storage and access patterns matter.

questions.q: How precise must estimates be?
questions.a: Order-of-magnitude accuracy with explicit assumptions is often more useful than unsupported precision.

questions.q: Why separate attempts from executions in capacity planning?
questions.a: A saved attempt is a storage event, while execution can have substantial CPU, memory, and time cost; their resource profiles differ.

questions.q: How should uncertainty affect an estimate?
questions.a: Use explicit ranges and sensitivity analysis, then identify which assumption most changes the design so it can be measured first.

lab: Estimate storage and peak QPS for one million learners with ten attempts per day. Include code snapshots and retention.

title: Caching and invalidation
summary: Make freshness a product decision.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Cache-aside reads first consult the cache and populate on a miss. Write-through and write-behind move write responsibilities differently. Every design needs a freshness budget, eviction policy, and failure behavior.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: A cache stampede occurs when many requests recompute the same expired value. Single-flight loading, jittered expiry, and serving bounded-stale values can reduce pressure. A hot key can remain a bottleneck even with many cache nodes.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For solution pages, content hashes support long-lived immutable caching. User progress requires stricter ownership and synchronization. Never reuse a public cache key for private personalized output.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Assume a lesson page takes 100 ms to compute and expires at noon. If 1,000 requests arrive immediately after expiry, naive cache-aside can create 1,000 recomputations, or 100 CPU-seconds of work if each cost is CPU time. A single-flight mechanism lets one request refresh while others await or receive a permitted stale value. Add randomized expiry so many different keys do not all expire together. If the page is immutable and addressed by a content hash, a new version gets a new key, simplifying invalidation without making personalized progress public.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Cache-aside can race with writes: a reader fetches old database data, a writer commits and invalidates, then the reader repopulates the cache with the old value. Versioned values or carefully designed update ordering can address the particular race. Negative caching reduces repeated misses but can hide newly created data until expiry. A high overall hit rate may conceal one expensive hot-key miss pattern. Measure miss cost and origin load, not only the hit percentage. Ensure fallback traffic is bounded when the cache becomes unavailable.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Draw the stale-repopulation interleaving and name the point where correctness fails. Specify keys, TTLs, invalidation, and whether stale responses are allowed for lessons versus progress. In a concurrency test, count origin calls during an expired-key burst and verify that single-flight actually coalesces work. Add a cache-outage scenario and show the load-limiting behavior. A passing test must include freshness and privacy checks as well as lower latency.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Request > Cache hit / miss > Origin > Populate

questions.q: Is a TTL a complete consistency strategy?
questions.a: No. It only bounds one source of staleness; concurrent writes and invalidation races still matter.

questions.q: What if the cache fails?
questions.a: The origin must tolerate fallback load or the service must degrade deliberately; unlimited fallback can cause a cascade.

questions.q: Why is a 99% hit rate not enough to prove a cache works well?
questions.a: The remaining misses may be unusually expensive, synchronized, or concentrated on critical keys; origin load and user latency still matter.

questions.q: When is stale-while-revalidate appropriate?
questions.a: When the product allows a bounded older representation while one refresh occurs, such as public lesson content, rather than strict fresh transactional state.

lab: Design cache keys for public lessons and private progress. Simulate 1,000 requests hitting one expired lesson.

title: Queues, Kafka, and delivery semantics
summary: Design consumers that tolerate retries.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A queue decouples producers from consumers and absorbs bursts within capacity. Kafka partitions provide ordered logs within each partition, not one universal order across all partitions. Partition keys affect ordering and load balance.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: At-least-once processing can repeat work after failures. Deduplication and idempotent writes make repetition safe. A database commit and an offset commit are separate events unless a specific transactional arrangement coordinates them.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For your payment system, use a transactional outbox to record business state and an event in one database transaction. The relay may resend; consumers still need deduplication keyed by an immutable event identifier.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A payment transaction writes payment P and outbox event E in the same database commit. A relay publishes E, then crashes before recording that publication. After restart it publishes E again. The consumer records E’s immutable identifier in a processed-events table inside the same transaction as its local effect. The second delivery finds that identifier and does not repeat the effect. This handles duplicate publication, but a remote side effect still needs its own idempotency or coordination. Walk through each commit separately rather than describing the whole pipeline as one atomic operation.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: An idempotency key needs a scope and retention policy. Reusing a key for different payloads should be rejected or explicitly handled, not silently treated as equivalent. A partition key preserving order for one account can create a hotspot for a very active account. Slow consumers accumulate lag, but increasing their count beyond the partition or downstream capacity will not fix throughput. Poison messages need a policy that preserves observability without indefinitely blocking unrelated work. Moving a message aside is an operational decision, not proof its business effect is complete.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create a crash matrix for before and after the business commit, publication, consumer effect, and offset commit. For every row, state whether retry produces a duplicate and where it is deduplicated. Show the unique constraint or transactional condition enforcing deduplication. Include a repeated key with a different payload and a consumer restart. Your success criterion is the correct business effect under retries, not merely a clean queue or an advanced offset.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Business transaction > Outbox > Kafka partition > Idempotent consumer

questions.q: Does exactly-once Kafka mean every external effect is once?
questions.a: No. External databases and services require compatible transaction or idempotency design.

questions.q: Why can adding consumers stop helping?
questions.a: Partition count, skew, downstream limits, or serial work can bound parallelism.

questions.q: Why store deduplication state with the consumer effect?
questions.a: If they commit separately, a crash can record one without the other, causing either repeated effects or skipped work.

questions.q: What does per-partition ordering imply for two accounts?
questions.a: Order is guaranteed within the relevant partition, but no universal order across independent partitions should be assumed.

lab: Enumerate crashes before and after database commit and offset commit. Show the resulting duplicate or lost-work risks.

title: Consistency, consensus, and partitions
summary: Choose behavior during communication failure.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Linearizability makes each operation appear to occur at one instant between invocation and response. Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence if updates eventually converge. Session guarantees occupy useful positions between these extremes.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: During a network partition, a system cannot guarantee both every request succeeds and a single consistent view under the CAP model. Consensus protocols such as Raft use replicated logs and quorums to agree despite some node failures.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: For a roster, stale analytics may be acceptable while assigning one bus to two drivers is not. Make consistency a per-operation requirement rather than labeling the whole product with one slogan.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: With five voting replicas, a majority requires three. In a 3–2 network split, the side with three can potentially continue committing under a correctly implemented majority consensus protocol; the side with two cannot safely form a majority. If two proposed majorities each have three members out of five, they overlap in at least one member. That intersection is necessary but not the whole proof: leader election rules and log consistency ensure the shared member cannot permit incompatible committed histories. Explain the protocol obligations instead of equating a head count with automatic correctness.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A healthy majority may still be unable to make progress temporarily during leader election, overloaded disks, or network instability. Consensus does not make client retries idempotent and does not automatically cover external side effects. Linearizable reads need an appropriate protocol to avoid a deposed leader serving stale data as current. Eventual consistency can be entirely suitable for activity feeds while unsuitable for exclusive resource assignment. Specify the operation’s invariant and failure behavior. Saying a database is simply CP or AP often hides configuration and per-operation distinctions.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Draw the five-node split, name the leader assumption, and show which acknowledgments are required. Explain what a client connected to the minority observes. Add a leader-failure case and distinguish temporary unavailability from an unsafe write. For the roster application, classify viewing statistics, editing notes, and assigning a bus by their consistency needs. State an acceptable stale-read window where relevant and justify where writes must be rejected instead of guessed.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Leader > Replicated log > Quorum > Committed state

questions.q: Is a majority enough for any arbitrary replication design?
questions.a: No. Quorum intersection alone does not establish protocol correctness, ordering, or safe leader changes.

questions.q: Why can a minority partition reject writes?
questions.a: It cannot establish the required quorum without risking conflicting histories.

questions.q: Why does quorum intersection not alone prove consensus?
questions.a: The protocol must also control leader authority, log ordering, and which entries may be acknowledged or committed across elections.

questions.q: Does consensus remove duplicate client operations?
questions.a: No. A client can retry an already committed command; application identifiers or state-machine deduplication are still needed.

lab: For five replicas split 3–2, explain which partition can commit under a majority consensus protocol and why.

title: Rate limits, retries, and resilience
summary: Prevent failure amplification.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: A token bucket allows controlled bursts while enforcing a long-term rate. A fixed-window counter is simple but can allow boundary bursts. Limits may apply per user, tenant, endpoint, and shared downstream resource.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Retries need deadlines, capped attempts, exponential backoff, and jitter. Retry only when the operation is safe and the failure is plausibly transient. Multiple layers each retrying can multiply traffic dramatically.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Circuit breakers stop repeated calls to a failing dependency; bulkheads isolate resource pools. Neither replaces capacity planning. Measure queue depth and saturation so overload is detected before every request times out.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A token bucket with capacity 20 and refill rate 5 tokens per second can accept an initial burst of 20 one-token requests, then sustain five per second. If 100 clients retry at exactly one second after a failure, the next burst can repeat the overload. Jitter spreads retries over an interval. If three service layers each make up to three attempts, one user request can create as many as 27 downstream attempts in the worst compounded pattern. Define a shared end-to-end deadline and decide which layer owns retries to avoid this multiplication.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Retrying quickly can turn a small outage into a cascading failure. A timeout budget should include queueing, connection setup, execution, and any retry delay. Circuit breakers need a recovery probe strategy; leaving a breaker permanently open prevents recovery, while admitting all traffic immediately can recreate overload. Per-user limits alone do not protect a shared dependency from many users acting together. Conversely, a single global limit can let one tenant consume all capacity. Combine fairness with a total resource budget and return a clear overload response.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Simulate an initial burst, steady traffic, and recovery after an outage. Verify the allowed burst and long-term rate independently.
