Record time to first token, inter-token latency, completed requests per second, memory use, and errors. Explain whether queueing or execution grows near saturation. If precision changes, rerun a correctness set. State hardware and runtime versions so results are interpretable. Your conclusion should name the workload favored by the chosen batching policy rather than report a context-free tokens-per-second number.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Request queue > Prefill > KV cache > Batched decode > Tokens

questions.q: Why retain a KV cache?
questions.a: It avoids recomputing previous tokens’ key and value representations during autoregressive decoding.

questions.q: Why is tokens per second alone insufficient?
questions.a: It hides queueing, first-token delay, concurrency, sequence lengths, and quality tradeoffs.

questions.q: Why can batching hurt interactive latency while improving efficiency?
questions.a: Requests may wait to share execution, and a larger batch can increase per-step work even as the hardware performs more total useful work.

questions.q: What limits the benefit of speculative decoding?
questions.a: Draft cost, verification cost, and the fraction of accepted draft tokens determine whether the extra work produces a net speedup.

lab: Design a benchmark matrix varying prompt length, output length, concurrency, and precision. Identify which metrics expose saturation.

title: Production deployment and model operations
summary: Treat an AI service as a versioned system.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Deployment includes model configuration, prompts, retrieval corpus, tool schemas, and runtime dependencies. Version these together so an incident can be reproduced and a change can be rolled back.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Use staged rollout and compare quality, latency, errors, and cost against a baseline. A fallback model must satisfy the same permission boundaries and output contract. Degrade explicitly when retrieval or a tool dependency is unavailable.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Monitor shifts in user questions and corpus freshness. Keep retention and access rules for logs, redact sensitive data, and define budgets. Re-run evaluations when changing providers or tools, not only when changing model weights.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Package release R17 with prompt hash P3, retriever version V5, corpus snapshot D12, tool schema T4, and model configuration M2. A canary sends five percent of eligible traffic to R17 while R16 remains available. If grounded-answer quality falls below the predeclared gate or p95 latency exceeds the budget, route new requests back to R16 and preserve traces for diagnosis. Rolling back only the application binary may fail if it still points at D12 or T4. Reproducibility requires the whole behavior-changing bundle and compatible state migrations.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A fallback provider can fail differently or return incompatible structured output. Do not broaden permissions or drop validation just to maintain apparent availability. A stale corpus may be worse than an explicit unavailable response for version-specific debugging. Logging everything improves apparent diagnosability but creates privacy and retention burdens. Keep operational metadata useful without collecting unnecessary source code or secrets. Canary samples may miss rare cases, so combine offline regression tests with live monitoring. A successful deployment includes an exercised rollback path rather than a document nobody has tried.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Write the complete version manifest and a rollout policy with measurable gates. Demonstrate a simulated retrieval-quality regression and route back to the previous compatible bundle. Include a tool-schema change and explain how old and new versions coexist during rollout. State which logs are retained and redacted. Your drill should measure time to detect and recover, verify representative user tasks afterward, and identify any state changes that cannot be undone by a simple binary rollback.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Versioned bundle > Evaluation > Canary > Monitor > Rollback

questions.q: What is a model deployment unit?
questions.a: Often more than weights: prompts, tools, retrieval data, configuration, and code jointly determine behavior.

questions.q: Why can a fallback worsen an incident?
questions.a: It may have different schemas, lower capacity, or unexpected latency and can overload a second dependency.

questions.q: Why version the corpus with the application behavior?
questions.a: Changed evidence can alter answers even when model and code are identical, so corpus identity is necessary for reproducing and attributing regressions.

questions.q: What makes a fallback acceptable?
questions.a: It must preserve required quality, permissions, output contracts, and capacity under the expected failure mode, rather than merely return any response.

lab: Write a rollout plan for a new RAG retriever with a rollback trigger and a test for stale document versions.

title: Your systems story: Linux and ARM64
summary: Turn debugging work into evidence of engineering judgment.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: Prepare one story around a concrete failure: expected behavior, observed symptom, impact, and your responsibility. Explain how you narrowed the problem across source, compiler, linker, ABI, and runtime boundaries.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: Use measurements and artifacts you can substantiate: a minimal reproducer, stack trace, disassembly, regression test, or upstream fix. Clearly distinguish your contribution from the team’s work and avoid inventing impact figures.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Practice a two-minute summary and a ten-minute technical version. Expect follow-ups on memory ordering, undefined behavior, optimization flags, and why the fix addresses the root cause rather than masking the symptom.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Use a hypothetical practice incident rather than inventing a resume claim: a C++ test passes in a debug build but crashes with optimization on ARM64. Start with a minimal input, record the compiler and flags, and reproduce the failure. Investigate object lifetime and undefined behavior before attributing it to code generation. Compare one variable at a time, inspect the faulting instruction, and connect its address back to source and ownership. Your final story should state which evidence ruled out alternatives and what regression test preserves the fix. Replace the hypothetical details only with facts from your actual experience.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: A polished story can become misleading if it compresses uncertainty into hindsight certainty. Say what you believed initially, what contradicted it, and how your hypothesis changed. Avoid attributing a team outcome entirely to yourself or inventing percentage improvements. Confidentiality does not require a vague answer: you can explain the failure class, debugging method, and validation without naming proprietary customers or code. An interviewer may challenge whether the issue was compiler, kernel, or application behavior. Welcome that distinction and show the evidence needed to cross each boundary.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Prepare a two-minute version containing problem, impact, your action, evidence, and outcome. Prepare a deeper version with a timeline, two rejected hypotheses, and the exact validation principle. Ask a practice partner to interrupt with why and how do you know questions. The story passes when you can distinguish observations from inferences, identify your contribution honestly, and explain a counterfactual: what would have happened if the suspected cause were different.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Symptom > Hypotheses > Reproducer > Evidence > Fix > Regression

questions.q: What if you cannot disclose proprietary details?
questions.a: Explain the technical pattern, your reasoning, and sanitized evidence without confidential identifiers or data.

questions.q: How do you show ownership?
questions.a: State the decisions and work you personally performed, collaboration involved, and how you verified the outcome.

questions.q: How do you discuss an incident when the original hypothesis was wrong?
questions.a: Explain the evidence that changed your mind and the improved experiment; disciplined correction demonstrates stronger debugging judgment than pretending you knew the answer immediately.

questions.q: What evidence makes a root-cause claim credible?
questions.a: A minimal reproducer, a mechanism explaining the symptom, a targeted fix, and a regression test that fails before and succeeds after the fix.

lab: Record a two-minute incident story. Have a practice partner challenge one assumption and ask for an alternative hypothesis.

title: Your product story: rosters, payments, and RAG
summary: Defend tradeoffs across three projects.

sections.heading: Understand
sections.body: For rostering, explain decision variables, hard constraints, soft objectives, and how infeasible inputs are handled. For analytics migration, describe reconciliation and workload-based storage choices. These show different forms of correctness.

sections.heading: Reason through a case
sections.body: For payments, trace one request through validation, transaction, event publication, consumer processing, and retry. For RAG, trace one question through retrieval, evidence selection, tool use, and evaluation. Name the boundary where each guarantee is enforced.

sections.heading: Interview edge
sections.body: Build a project evidence sheet with architecture, one difficult bug, a rejected alternative, a measurement, and a future improvement. Company-specific interviews vary; use this foundation to adapt to the role’s published requirements rather than assuming a fixed company question list.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: For a rostering practice example, define binary x[d,s] indicating driver d assigned to shift s. Require exactly one driver per shift, at most one overlapping shift per driver, and a maximum weekly workload. A soft objective can minimize imbalance. If coverage and availability conflict, the solver should report infeasibility rather than quietly break a hard constraint. For payments, trace one idempotency key through database and events. For RAG, trace one claim back to retrieved evidence. These examples share a theme: define the invariant first, then identify the component that enforces it.

sections.heading: Failure modes and tradeoffs
sections.body: Project interviews often expose gaps between a diagram and actual ownership. Be ready to explain a schema, failure path, and rejected alternative rather than only list frameworks. Constraint optimization needs clear distinctions between feasible and optimal; a time-limited solver may find a feasible solution without proving optimality. Payment retries and RAG citations similarly require exact semantics rather than labels. Do not assume a company always asks a fixed question set. Adapt emphasis to the published role and your strongest verified experience while preserving broad coding and fundamentals practice.

sections.heading: Lab acceptance criteria
sections.body: Create one page per project with problem, constraints, architecture, one failure, one measurement, and one improvement. Include the rostering objective and hard constraints, the payment crash matrix, and a RAG failure taxonomy. Rehearse a 35-minute design discussion followed by a 10-minute critique. The rubric rewards explicit assumptions, correct guarantees, honest ownership, and evidence. Any numerical impact claim must be supported by a measurement you actually made or clearly labeled as a hypothetical estimate.

diagram.caption: Conceptual flow: Problem > Constraint > Decision > Failure mode > Evidence > Learning

questions.q: How do you discuss a project without impressive metrics?
questions.a: Use honest evidence of correctness, complexity, test coverage, or operational behavior and explain what you would measure next.

questions.q: How do you answer why multi-agent?
questions.a: Explain the measured benefit of separation, or acknowledge when a simpler workflow is preferable.

questions.q: What is the difference between feasible and optimal in rostering?
questions.a: Feasible satisfies all hard constraints; optimal additionally achieves the best objective value under the model, with proof depending on solver status and completion.

questions.q: How do you answer a framework-choice question convincingly?
questions.a: Connect the choice to a concrete requirement, compare a credible alternative, and explain the observed benefit and the cost you accepted.

lab: Prepare one diagram and five adversarial follow-up questions for each project. Rehearse with a 35-minute design and 10-minute critique.
